items.title: fastfields
items.text:
fastfields is the one-import way to use the toolkit: fastfields.auto looks at whatever array you hand it — NumPy or PyTorch — and runs the operation on the matching backend. Write your code once and it works across frameworks.

One pip install fastfields gives you all of it: fastfields.auto plus the per-framework modules fastfields.numpy, fastfields.torch and fastfields.cupy, and the shared fastfields.helpers. Only the backends you install are loaded, so fastfields[numpy] alone is a perfectly good setup. Today the tested, working path is CPU (NumPy and PyTorch); the CuPy/GPU path is implemented but not yet published as a wheel or validated on hardware — see Status below.

This is the Python section of the fastfields documentation. The project overview has the per-operation status matrix and the roadmap; the layers underneath are documented separately, as the raw DLPack binding and the C++/CUDA library.

items.title: Install
items.text:
# CPU (NumPy)
pip install "fastfields[numpy]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/

Use fastfields[torch] for PyTorch, or fastfields[all] for all three.

The extra picks the array library; the --extra-index-url picks the compiled fastfields-dlpack lane. Those are two separate choices, and the second one is the one that matters for GPU work — see the monorepo note. A GPU (CuPy / CUDA) wheel lane is planned but not published yet — see Status.

items.title: Use it
items.text:
import numpy as np
from fastfields import auto as ff

mask = np.zeros((256, 256), "float32")
mask[:, 128] = 1.0

dist = ff.dt_euclidean(mask)      # dispatched to the NumPy backend

import torch
tmask = torch.zeros(256, 256)
tmask[:, 128] = 1.0
tdist = ff.dt_euclidean(tmask)    # same call, dispatched to PyTorch

items.title: What's inside
items.text:
Operation Functions Distance transforms dt_euclidean, dt_l1; point-to-spline dt_spline_table / dt_spline_brent / dt_spline_gaussnewton; point-to-mesh dt_mesh Positive-definite linear algebra sym_matvec, sym_matvec_backward, sym_solve, sym_invert over whole fields of small symmetric matrices Resampling resample (spline up/down-sampling), restriction (its adjoint), spline_coeff (coefficient prefilter) Pushpull pull / push (spline gather & its adjoint scatter), count, grad — the building blocks of image warping/sampling Regularisers field_matvec / flow_matvec (absolute / membrane / bending energies on fields & vector flows) and their *_diag preconditioners

Each call forwards straight to the selected backend, so it shares that backend's signature and behaviour (autograd on PyTorch, CUDA streams on CuPy). Prefer a single framework? Use fastfields.numpy, fastfields.torch or fastfields.cupy directly — they are in the same install.

In-place spellings are dispatched too (dt_euclidean_, sym_solve_, spline_coeff_, the *_add…_/*_sub…_ accumulate forms): they mutate their first argument, which is also the array the backend is chosen from.

items.title: What is not dispatched here, and why
items.text:
fastfields.auto picks a backend from the type of the first array argument and forwards everything unchanged. Two kinds of operation cannot be reached through it, and both are deliberate.

Builders that take a shape, not an array — field_diag, flow_diag, field_kernel, flow_kernel allocate their output from a rank and a set of penalty weights, so there is no array to dispatch on. Call them on a concrete backend and pass the result into the dispatched operators. Their *_add…/*_sub… accumulate forms do take an array and are dispatched.

Adjoints that exist for autograd — pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward are the gradients of the pushpull operators. Only fastfields.torch has an autograd engine, and there they are wired into the forward op's autograd.Function rather than exported, so there is nothing uniform to dispatch. Call fastfields.auto.pull(...) on a torch tensor and .backward(), or reach for fastfields.dlpack raw.

Operations only some backends have are still dispatched, with a partial table that raises NotImplementedError naming the backends that do have them: field_cg (CPU-only in the C++ library, so numpy), field_precond_ / flow_precond_ (numpy and cupy), sym_matvec_backward (numpy and cupy). Listing them with a clear failure beats omitting them, which would make the asymmetry invisible from here.

And if a backend turns out not to have an operation this module says it does — a mixed install, where fastfields.auto is newer than the wrapper — the call raises NotImplementedError saying which package to upgrade, not a bare AttributeError from a module you never named.

dt_spline_* returns (dist, time) on every backend

The three point-to-spline operators return a 2-tuple, and all three namespaces return it in that order. fastfields.cupy returned (time, dist) until fastfields#38: a dispatcher that forwards arguments unchanged has nowhere to normalise a result, so the meaning of a dispatched return value depended on which array type you passed. The three names are part of the canonical surface the cross-backend conformance suite checks, so a namespace cannot quietly drift again.

Their signatures agreed later than their return order did. fastfields.cupy spelled the spline order spline and made max_iter/tol/step required positional arguments, where numpy and torch had keyword-only order/bound with defaults. All three now use the numpy/torch spelling, and signature drift — parameter names, kinds, order, defaults — fails CI in tests/test_signature_conformance.py rather than at a user's call.

items.title: Status
items.text:
fastfields is alpha. The table below is what is actually exposed and tested today, mirroring the candour of the internal migration matrix — so you know before you install.

Operation NumPy (CPU) PyTorch (CPU) CuPy (GPU) Distance — Euclidean / L1 ✅ ✅ 🧭 Distance — point-to-mesh / point-to-spline 🧪 🧪¹ 🧭 Positive-definite linear algebra (sym_*) ✅ ✅ 🧭 Resampling (resample / restriction / spline_coeff) ✅ ✅ 🧭 Pushpull (spline gather / scatter / grad) ✅ ✅ 🧭 Regularisers (membrane / bending energies) ✅ ✅ 🧭

✅ works, covered by the CPU test suite  ·  🧪 exposed but not yet covered by tests (shape contracts still being firmed up — use with care)  ·  🧭 planned (see below).

¹ PyTorch exposes point-to-mesh (dt_mesh) but not the point-to-spline variants.

What "planned" means here:

  • GPU / CuPy (the only remaining 🧭). The CUDA kernels and the CuPy wrapper exist and compile + link — every op family, pushpull and the regularisers included, is exposed on all three backends — but there is no GPU in CI, so no GPU wheel is published yet and nothing has run on real hardware. The wheel lanes are deferred until that changes.

Everything marked ✅ is exercised by a brute-force reference test on CPU.

See the API reference for full signatures and options, and one distribution, five namespaces for how the packaging fits together.

items.title: fastfields.auto
items.text:
fastfields.auto is the backend-dispatching interface: every function looks at the type of the first array argument and forwards the call, unchanged, to the matching per-framework package. Write the call once and it runs on whichever array library the caller happens to be using.

you pass it calls numpy.ndarray fastfields.numpy torch.Tensor fastfields.torch cupy.ndarray fastfields.cupy

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install "fastfields[numpy]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/

fastfields.auto ships with the fastfields distribution and needs no extra of its own — but it has nothing to dispatch to until at least one backend is installed, so pick the extra for the array library you use ([numpy], [torch], [cupy], or [all]). It dispatches over exactly the subset you installed.

items.title: Use it
items.text:
import numpy as np
from fastfields import auto as ff

mask = np.zeros((256, 256), "float32")
mask[:, 128] = 1.0

dist = ff.dt_euclidean(mask)      # -> runs on fastfields.numpy

Hand the same function a torch.Tensor and it runs on fastfields.torch instead, with autograd, and returns a tensor. Arguments are forwarded unchanged, so each call has the signature of the backend function it selects — spline order and boundary arguments accept an int, a Spline / Bound enum, or a string like "cubic" or "dct2", exactly as they do on a concrete backend.

items.title: When to use it, and when to use a backend directly
items.text:
Reach for fastfields.auto when the array type is not yours to choose: library code that must accept whatever its caller hands it, a function that runs over both NumPy and PyTorch data, or a script you want to move between CPU and GPU without rewriting imports.

Use fastfields.numpy, fastfields.torch or fastfields.cupy directly when you already know the array type. You get a typed API, the backend's own documented signatures, and an import error at import time rather than a dispatch error on first call. Nothing is lost by doing so — fastfields.auto adds dispatch, not capability, and every operation it reaches is an operation one of those three already has.

items.title: Backends are imported lazily
items.text:
Detection is by the array type's top-level module name, so importing fastfields.auto does not import NumPy, PyTorch or CuPy — only the backend for an array you actually pass gets imported, and only once. That is what makes it usable with any subset of the backends installed.

The failures are correspondingly specific:

  • an object that is not a NumPy, PyTorch or CuPy array raises TypeError naming the type it was given;
  • an array whose backend package (or that package's own dependency) is not installed raises ImportError naming what to install;
  • an operation a backend does not have raises NotImplementedError naming the backends that do have it — never a bare AttributeError from a module the caller never mentioned.

items.title: What it does not dispatch
items.text:
Two kinds of operation cannot be reached through fastfields.auto, both deliberately:

  • Builders that take a shape, not an array. field_diag, flow_diag, field_kernel and flow_kernel allocate their output from a rank and a set of penalty weights, so there is no array to dispatch on. Call them on a concrete backend and pass the result into the dispatched operators. Their *_add… / *_sub… accumulate forms do take an array and are dispatched.
  • Adjoints that exist for autograd. pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward are wired into fastfields.torch's autograd.Function rather than exported, since only PyTorch has an autograd engine. The supported spelling is fastfields.auto.pull(...) followed by .backward() on a torch tensor.

A few operations exist on some backends only and are dispatched with a partial table, raising NotImplementedError that names the backends which have them: field_cg (numpy), field_precond_ / flow_precond_ and sym_matvec_backward (numpy and cupy). Listing them with a clear failure keeps the asymmetry visible.

items.title: Which lane am I on?
items.text:
fastfields.auto never requires a particular compute backend — unlike fastfields.cupy, which refuses to import on a CPU-only build, and fastfields.torch, which refuses a CUDA tensor on one. It only reports:

from fastfields import auto as ff

ff.dlpack_backend()      # "cpu", "cu126", ... or None

None means the installed fastfields-dlpack build carries no lane label, or that it cannot be imported at all. Only the CPU lane is published today, so fastfields.cupy and CUDA torch tensors are not usable yet — see the project status matrix.

See the API reference for the full list of dispatched operations and their signatures.

items.title: fastfields.cupy
items.text:
fastfields.cupy runs the fastfields field operators on the GPU, straight on your CuPy arrays. Same API as the NumPy package, but the work happens in device memory and is ordered on CuPy's current CUDA stream.

CuPy itself isn't installed automatically — the right build depends on your CUDA version — so pull it in with the cupy extra (or install a matching cupy-cuda12x yourself).

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install "fastfields[cupy]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cu130/

!!! warning "The extra selects CuPy; the index URL selects the CUDA kernels"

These are two separate choices and only the second one can fail
quietly. `pip install "fastfields[cupy]"` installs CuPy and
succeeds against a **CPU-only** `fastfields-dlpack`, because
`pip` has no way to say "any build with CUDA" -- the lane comes
from the index folder you point it at. `import fastfields.cupy`
then fails immediately, with a message naming the lane to
install, because there is no CPU path here to fall back to.
See [the monorepo note](monorepo.md) for why it works this way.

No `cu*` lane is published yet. Until one is, this install has
nothing to resolve to -- the
[index](https://fastfields.github.io/whl/) lists the lanes that actually exist.

items.title: Use it
items.text:
import cupy as cp
import fastfields.cupy as ff

mask = cp.zeros((256, 256), "float32")
mask[:, 128] = 1.0

dist = ff.dt_euclidean(mask)      # new array; mask is untouched
ff.dt_euclidean_(mask)            # in-place variant, writes into mask

items.title: What's inside
items.text:
Operation Functions Distance transforms dt_euclidean, dt_l1 (along the last axis); point-to-spline dt_spline_table / dt_spline_brent / dt_spline_gaussnewton; point-to-mesh dt_mesh Positive-definite linear algebra sym_matvec, sym_addmatvec_, sym_submatvec_, sym_solve, sym_invert over whole fields of small symmetric matrices Resampling resample (spline up/down-sampling), restriction (its adjoint), spline_coeff (coefficient prefilter) Spline gather/scatter pull, push, count, grad Regularisers field_* (multi-channel field, per-channel penalties) and flow_* (vector flow, scalar penalties + the Lamé shears/div terms): the operator *_matvec, its diagonal *_diag, its stencil *_kernel, the *_add…/*_sub… accumulate forms of each, the RLS/JRLS-weighted *_rls variants, and the regularised system below

Functional wrappers (dt_euclidean, sym_matvec, …) allocate their outputs and return new arrays; the trailing-underscore variants (dt_euclidean_, sym_solve_, …) write in place. To target a specific stream, wrap the call in a with my_stream: block.

items.title: Solving the regularised system
items.text:
With H the per-voxel data-term Hessian (compact-symmetric packing) and L a regulariser:

call what it does field_forward / flow_forward apply (H + L) x field_precond / flow_precond apply (H + diag(L))⁻¹ g (Jacobi) field_precond_ / flow_precond_ the same, in place field_relax / flow_relax Gauss-Seidel sweeps on (H + L) x = g

Each is one fused kernel, so none of them allocates a temporary you then have to keep alive until the stream is synchronised.

items.title: What this wrapper does not expose
items.text:
Of the 58 operations in the underlying C++ hub, this package wraps all but five.

pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward are the adjoints of the gather/scatter operators with respect to both the sampled field and the sampling coordinates. They exist so an autograd engine can differentiate through grid — which only fastfields.torch does. There is no automatic differentiation on cupy, so they stay at the raw layer: call fastfields.dlpack.pull_backward(...) if you need them.

field_cg — the conjugate-gradient solver — is CPU-only in the underlying library: its dot products need a device-side reduction the CUDA backend does not implement yet (fastfields-lib#34), and the hub rejects CUDA arrays rather than quietly running on the host. A fastfields.cupy.field_cg could therefore only ever raise, so there isn't one. Use field_relax, which does run on CUDA and solves the same system by Gauss-Seidel sweeps.

tests/test_api_coverage.py fails if that list ever changes by accident, and it runs without a GPU.

See the API reference for full signatures and options.

items.title: fastfields.helpers
items.text: fastfields.helpers is the shared, dependency-free Python layer of the fastfields stack: the Spline and Bound enums, and the argument-normalisation helpers used by fastfields.numpy, fastfields.torch, fastfields.cupy and the fastfields.auto dispatcher.

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install fastfields

It ships with the fastfields distribution; there is nothing extra to install for it. The module itself imports only the standard library -- no array backend, and none of the compiled bindings.

items.title: Use it
items.text:
from fastfields.helpers import Spline, Bound, as_spline, as_bound

as_spline("cubic")        # 3
as_bound("wrap")          # 6  == int(Bound.DFT)
as_spline(Spline.Linear)  # 1

items.title: Why it exists
items.text:
These helpers used to live inside fastfields-dlpack, next to the compiled nanobind extension, so a one-line fix to a string alias or a rounding rule could only reach users through a full compiled-wheel release cycle on every platform. They were split out to escape that, and the escape survives the merge: they now ship in the fastfields distribution, which is still a single universal (py3-none-any) wheel with no compiled content, so a fix to them is still an ordinary pure-Python release.

What this module may depend on has not changed either: nothing. It imports no array library and, in particular, never fastfields.dlpack -- a subprocess test enforces that.

items.title: What's inside
items.text:
Group Names Enums Spline (orders 0–7), Bound (8 boundary conditions) Normalisers as_spline, as_bound — accept an int, an enum member or a friendly string Shape / ndim normalize_shape, infer_ndim, check_ndim, resolve_out_spatial Anchors anchor_scale_shift — torch-interpol anchor → per-dim scale + scalar shift

See the API reference for full signatures and options.

items.title: One distribution, five namespaces
items.text:
fastfields used to be five separate PyPI distributions, one per subpackage of the fastfields namespace:

was shipped now fastfields-helpers fastfields.helpers fastfields fastfields-numpy fastfields.numpy fastfields fastfields-cupy fastfields.cupy fastfields fastfields-torch fastfields.torch fastfields fastfields fastfields.auto fastfields fastfields-dlpack fastfields.dlpack fastfields-dlpack (unchanged)

They are now one distribution, fastfields, shipping all five. Nothing about the import surface moved: the same five fastfields.<sub> modules exist, with the same contents, and fastfields.dlpack still merges into the same namespace from its own wheel.

items.title: What stayed the same, deliberately
items.text:
They are still PEP 420 namespace subpackages. There is no fastfields/__init__.py anywhere, in this distribution or in fastfields-dlpack. That absence is the whole mechanism: fastfields is a native namespace package, so two independently-installed wheels can each contribute a fastfields/<sub>/ directory and both be importable. Add a top-level __init__.py and fastfields becomes an ordinary package owned by whichever wheel shipped it -- and fastfields.dlpack, the compiled half, stops being importable. The merged pyproject.toml lists each subpackage explicitly with namespaces = true for exactly this reason, and tools/consolidate-python.sh fails if an __init__.py ever appears there.

fastfields-dlpack stays a separate distribution and a separate repo. It is the only compiled one: it needs a per-platform wheel matrix, and libfastfields-cpu.so alone is about 166 MB. Folding it in would mean every one-line Python fix rebuilds and re-uploads that whole matrix -- which is exactly why fastfields-helpers was split out of it in the first place. Merging the five pure-Python distributions keeps that property: fastfields is still one universal py3-none-any wheel with no compiled content, so a fix to any of the five ships as an ordinary pure-Python release. There is no circularity to worry about either -- fastfields-dlpack depends only on packaging, never on anything here.

The array libraries are still optional. numpy, torch and cupy are extras (fastfields[numpy], [torch], [cupy], [all]), so pip install fastfields works with whatever subset you have, and fastfields.auto dispatches over exactly that subset. fastfields-dlpack is the only hard dependency.

items.title: The one wrinkle: an extra is not a lane
items.text:
This is the part worth reading before filing a bug.

fastfields-dlpack encodes which compute backend it was compiled for in its version's PEP 440 local segment, PyTorch-style: 0.0.dev0+cpu, +cu118, +cu126, +cu130. It exposes that at runtime as fastfields.dlpack.backend. Which one you get is decided by the index folder you install from, not by the dependency graph:

pip install fastfields --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/
pip install fastfields --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cu130/

No package in this distribution pins a lane, and none can: pip has no way to express "any build with CUDA", and a pin would fight the --extra-index-url you just chose. So the dependency on fastfields-dlpack is deliberately unqualified.

The consequence is that the cupy extra selects the CuPy client library, not the CUDA lane:

pip install "fastfields[cupy]"      # succeeds -- on the CPU lane too
python -c "import fastfields.cupy"  # ImportError

That install is not wrong in any way pip can see, and it is not a resolution failure. It is a mismatch that only the package itself can detect, so each namespace enforces its own requirement at runtime:

namespace needs what it does fastfields.numpy CPU nothing. The CPU path works on any build. fastfields.cupy CUDA fails at import if fastfields.dlpack.backend is not cu*. Every operation here runs in CUDA device memory, so there is no partial mode worth offering. The message names the index URL and the pip command. fastfields.torch either fails lazily: the CPU path is the tested one and runs on any build, so the import always succeeds and the check happens only when a CUDA tensor arrives (in stream_ptr, which every operation already calls). fastfields.auto whatever is installed reports. fastfields.auto.dlpack_backend() returns the label; dispatch is dynamic already.

An unlabelled build (backend is None, which is what an unversioned source checkout reports) is let through everywhere. It means unknown, not CPU, and every wheel from the index carries a real label -- so refusing it would block GPU development from a source tree while catching no real mistake.

items.title: How the merge was done
items.text:
tools/consolidate-python.sh is the frozen record, and the Python-side sibling of fastfields-lib's tools/consolidate.sh. In outline: one git filter-repo path-move pass per absorbed repo, then four --allow-unrelated-histories merges into this repo's existing history. This repo was not rewritten, so its main is still a true ancestor of the result and every existing commit SHA and permalink against it still resolves.

History is preserved, including across the old fastfields_numpy/ -> fastfields/numpy/ layout rename, which the path rules fold onto one path so git log --follow crosses it. Issue and PR numbers do not transfer: GitHub does not redirect them across a repository merge, so a reference to, say, fastfields-numpy#23 remains a reference to that archived repo.

items.title: fastfields.numpy
items.text: fastfields.numpy brings the fastfields field operators to plain NumPy arrays on the CPU. Every function takes NumPy arrays in and returns fresh NumPy arrays out — your inputs are left untouched unless you explicitly ask for an in-place variant.

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install "fastfields[numpy]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/

The numpy extra pulls NumPy itself; the fastfields distribution ships this subpackage along with fastfields.torch, fastfields.cupy, fastfields.auto and fastfields.helpers. The --extra-index-url is what selects the compiled fastfields-dlpack lane -- cpu is the right one here.

items.title: Use it
items.text:
import numpy as np
import fastfields.numpy as ff

mask = np.zeros((256, 256), "float32")
mask[:, 128] = 1.0

dist = ff.dt_euclidean(mask)      # squared Euclidean distance along the last axis

items.title: fastfields.torch
items.text: fastfields.torch brings the fastfields field operators to PyTorch, and the core operations are fully differentiable — drop them into a model and gradients flow straight through. Functions take and return torch tensors and allocate their own outputs.

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install "fastfields[torch]" \
    --extra-index-url https://fastfields.github.io/whl/cpu/

CPU tensors work on any build. A CUDA tensor needs a CUDA build of fastfields-dlpack, which means installing from a cu* lane of the index instead of cpu/; pass one and the same code runs on the GPU. Hand a CUDA tensor to a CPU-only build and the call raises a RuntimeError naming the lane to install -- it is checked when the tensor arrives, not at import, precisely so that the CPU path keeps working everywhere.

items.title: Use it
items.text:
import torch
import fastfields.torch as ff

mat = torch.randn(5, 6, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)  # packed C=3
vec = torch.randn(5, 3, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)

out = ff.sym_matvec(mat, vec)     # H @ vec, differentiable
out.sum().backward()              # gradients land on mat and vec

items.title: What's inside
items.text: Operation Functions Positive-definite linear algebra sym_matvec, sym_solve (differentiable); sym_invert, sym_addmatvec_, sym_submatvec_ over whole fields of small symmetric matrices Resampling resample (spline up/down-sampling), restriction (its adjoint), spline_coeff (coefficient prefilter) — all differentiable Spline gather/scatter pull, push, count, grad — all differentiable with respect to the sampling grid Distance transforms dt_euclidean, dt_l1, dt_mesh, and point-to-spline dt_spline_table / dt_spline_brent / dt_spline_gaussnewton Regularisers field_* (multi-channel field, per-channel penalties) and flow_* (vector flow, scalar penalties + the Lamé shears/div terms): the operator *_matvec, its diagonal *_diag, its stencil *_kernel, the *_add…/*_sub… accumulate forms of each, the RLS/JRLS-weighted *_rls variants, *_relax, and *_forward / *_precond

items.title: What is differentiable
items.text:
Differentiable: sym_matvec, sym_solve, resample, restriction, spline_coeff, all four pushpull operators (pull, push, count, grad — with respect to the field and the sampling coordinates), and the regulariser operators including field_forward / field_precond and their flow twins.

grad deserves a note: it is itself a derivative operator, so differentiating it produces second-order terms — which is the point, since an image gradient computed inside a loss has to be differentiable for the deformation that produced grid to be learnable. Its abs=True mode is a majorisation, and its backward is the adjoint of the majorised operator rather than a true Jacobian; use it as the majorisation it is.

Not differentiable, but exposed for parity with fastfields.numpy / fastfields.cupy: the distance transforms (dt_euclidean, dt_l1, dt_mesh, the three dt_spline_*), sym_invert, and the mat/vec gradients of sym_addmatvec_ / sym_submatvec_. Forward always runs, even when an input requires grad; only calling .backward() through the output raises, with a RuntimeError naming the op.

items.title: What this wrapper does not expose
items.text:
Of the 58 operations in the underlying C++ hub this package wraps all but nine, and the nine split into two groups.

Adjoints that are used, not re-exported. pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward, grad_backward and sym_matvec_backward are the gradients behind the autograd.Function of each forward op, which is the supported way to reach them: call the forward op and .backward(). Re-exporting them would be a second, unchecked spelling of a gradient, with five pre-zeroed buffers and an accumulate-vs-overwrite contract for the caller to get right. fastfields.dlpack has them raw.

Three solver entry points that need an autograd decision first. field_precond_ and flow_precond_ are in-place preconditioner solves, and field_cg runs an iterative solver whose gradient is a solve with the same operator. Both are worth doing and neither is a mechanical wrapper, so they are deliberately not here yet; field_relax is the in-place solver available today, and fastfields.numpy has all three for the non-autograd case.

tests/test_api_coverage.py fails if that list ever changes by accident.

See the API reference for full signatures and options.

items.title: API reference
items.text:
The fastfields distribution ships five subpackages of the fastfields namespace. Pick the one matching the arrays you work with, or fastfields.auto to let it dispatch for you.

Page Module For auto fastfields.auto dispatches on the array type you pass numpy fastfields.numpy NumPy arrays, CPU torch fastfields.torch PyTorch tensors, with autograd cupy fastfields.cupy CuPy arrays in CUDA device memory helpers fastfields.helpers the shared Spline/Bound enums and argument normalisers

The raw bindings they are all built on, fastfields.dlpack, ship from a separate distribution (fastfields-dlpack) and are documented there.

items.title: fastfields.auto

items.title: fastfields.auto
items.text:
fastfields.auto: a backend-dispatching interface over fastfields wrappers.

Every function here dispatches on the type of the first array argument and forwards the call to the matching backend package:

  • numpy.ndarray -> :mod:fastfields.numpy
  • torch.Tensor -> :mod:fastfields.torch
  • cupy.ndarray -> :mod:fastfields.cupy

Backends are imported lazily: only the backend for the array type actually passed is imported, so fastfields.auto works with any subset of the optional backends installed (only fastfields-helpers -- the pure-Python enums/normalisers, no compiled extension -- is a hard dependency; fastfields.auto never touches the compiled fastfields-dlpack bindings directly). A clear error is raised for an unknown array type, and a clear ImportError if the required backend package (or its own dependency, e.g. torch/cupy) is missing.

Every backend wrapper package exposes the same canonical dt_* / sym_* names, and this module exposes one unified name per operation that maps to each backend's function. Arguments are forwarded unchanged, so each dispatched call shares the signature of the selected backend's function.

This namespace requires no particular compute backend -- it runs against whatever is installed, and :func:dlpack_backend reports which lane that is ("cpu", "cu126", ...). That is the whole of its backend handling, by contrast with :mod:fastfields.cupy, which refuses to import on a CPU-only build, and :mod:fastfields.torch, which refuses a CUDA tensor on one.

The dispatchers are split by category into :mod:._dt (distance transforms), :mod:._sym (compact-symmetric ops), :mod:._resample (resampling / spline coefficients), :mod:._pushpull (spline gather/scatter) and :mod:._reg (spatial regularisers), all built on the shared machinery in :mod:._util.

What is not dispatched here, and why

This module is a dispatcher: it picks a backend from the type of the first array argument and forwards every argument unchanged. Two kinds of operation cannot be reached through it, and both are deliberate.

Builders that take a shape, not an array. field_diag, flow_diag, field_kernel and flow_kernel allocate their output from a rank and a set of penalty weights -- there is no array to dispatch on, so there is nothing for this module to decide. Call them on a concrete backend (fastfields.numpy.field_diag(...)) and pass the result into the dispatched operators. Their *_add/*_sub accumulate forms do take an array and are dispatched.

Adjoints that exist for autograd. pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward and grad_backward are the gradients of the pushpull operators; only :mod:fastfields.torch has an autograd engine, and there they are wired into the forward op's autograd.Function rather than exported. There is nothing uniform to dispatch, so the supported spelling is fastfields.auto.pull(...) followed by .backward() on a torch tensor, or fastfields.dlpack.pull_backward(...) raw.

Operations that some backends have are dispatched with a partial table and raise NotImplementedError naming the backends that do have them -- field_cg (CPU-only in the C++ library, so numpy), field_precond_ / flow_precond_ (numpy and cupy), sym_matvec_backward (numpy and cupy). Listing them with a clear failure is better than omitting them, which would make the asymmetry invisible from here.

If a backend turns out not to have an operation this module says it does -- a mixed install, where fastfields.auto is newer than the wrapper -- the call raises NotImplementedError saying which package to upgrade, not a bare AttributeError from a module the caller never named.

items.title: fastfields.cupy
items.text:
fastfields.cupy: a user-friendly cupy interface over fastfields.dlpack.

This package mirrors the numpy-style fastfields interface but operates on cupy arrays living in CUDA device memory. The underlying fastfields.dlpack functions accept any object exposing __dlpack__ (cupy arrays do, sharing device memory with zero copy) and write results in place or through pre-allocated outputs.

Conventions
  • Functional wrappers (dt_euclidean, sym_matvec, resample ...) take cupy arrays, allocate their outputs, and return cupy arrays. Inputs must be float32/float64 but are passed with their native strides (the stride-aware C++/CUDA library reads them zero-copy -- no contiguous copy is forced); freshly allocated outputs are always contiguous.
  • Trailing-underscore wrappers (dt_euclidean_, sym_solve_ ...) operate in place / through the caller's output array and return it.
  • Streams: cupy queues work on its current CUDA stream. Every wrapper forwards cupy.cuda.get_current_stream().ptr to the binding's stream argument, so the C++/CUDA kernels are correctly ordered w.r.t. the surrounding cupy operations. To run on a specific stream, wrap the call in a with my_stream: block.
Availability

Two different things can be missing, and they are treated differently.

  • The cupy client library. Imported lazily, so import fastfields.cupy succeeds where cupy itself is not installed or no GPU is present; a clear ImportError is raised only when a wrapper is actually called. This is what lets the static parts of this package (the enums, the argument normalisation) be imported and tested anywhere.
  • The CUDA kernels. Checked eagerly: import fastfields.cupy raises ImportError when the installed fastfields-dlpack is a CPU-only build, naming the wheel-index lane to install instead. Unlike a missing cupy, that is not a situation any part of this package can work in -- see :mod:fastfields.cupy._backend.
What this wrapper deliberately does not expose

Of the 58 public operations of the C++ hub, this package wraps all but five. tools/api_inventory.py in fastfields-dlpack prints the full matrix; the omissions are:

pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward, grad_backward The adjoints of the pushpull operators, with respect to both the sampled field and the sampling coordinates. They exist so that an autograd engine can differentiate through grid, which only :mod:fastfields.torch has; there is no automatic differentiation on cupy, so a wrapper here would be a bare function nothing calls, with five pre-zeroed device buffers for the caller to get right -- and, on CUDA, five more blocks to keep alive until the stream is synchronised. They stay reachable through the raw bindings: fastfields.dlpack.pull_backward(...).

field_cg The conjugate-gradient driver is CPU-only in fastfields-lib: the solver's dot products need a device-side reduction the CUDA backend does not implement yet (fastfields-lib#34), and the hub rejects CUDA tensors rather than silently running on the host. A fastfields.cupy.field_cg could therefore only ever raise, so this package does not pretend to have one. :func:field_relax and :func:flow_relax do run on CUDA and solve the same system by Gauss-Seidel sweeps; when fastfields-lib#34 lands, wrapping field_cg here is a two-screen change and tests/test_api_coverage.py will remind whoever is looking.

This is checked rather than asserted: tests/test_api_coverage.py fails if the set of operations this package omits ever differs from the list above.

Return the pointer of cupy's current CUDA stream.

fastfields_bind forwards its stream argument straight to the CUDA backend, so every wrapper passes this value. items.title: fastfields.helpers
items.text:
Shared enums and argument-normalisation helpers for the fastfields packages.

The fastfields.numpy / fastfields.torch / fastfields.cupy wrappers and the fastfields.auto dispatcher all need the same backend-agnostic logic: the :class:Spline / :class:Bound enums, the order/bound normalisers, and the resolution of factor/shape/anchor into the per-dim scale + scalar shift that the resize binding consumes. It lives here, in one dependency-free package, so each consumer imports it instead of carrying its own copy.

This package is pure Python and dependency-free -- it imports nothing but the standard library, and in particular no numpy/torch/cupy and none of the compiled fastfields.dlpack bindings. That is the point of it existing separately: a fix to any of this logic ships as an ordinary pure-Python release, with no recompilation of the C++/CUDA chain and no per-platform wheel cycle.

fastfields.helpers is a sibling of fastfields.dlpack, not a layer over it -- neither package depends on the other.

items.title: fastfields.numpy
items.text:
fastfields.numpy: a friendly numpy interface over fastfields.dlpack.

The underlying bindings operate in place / write through pre-allocated output arrays. This package wraps them so every public function takes numpy arrays and returns freshly allocated numpy arrays, never clobbering the caller's input -- unless it is one of the trailing-underscore (_) variants, e.g. dt_euclidean_/sym_solve_/spline_coeff_, which mutate their first argument in place and return it. This mirrors the cupy backend's convention exactly (fastfields.cupy's docstring: "Trailing-underscore wrappers ... operate in place"); torch omits the in-place spelling for ops whose backward would need the pre-mutation value (see API_CONTRACT.md, "In-place policy").

Batch (leading) dimensions are broadcast: the raw bindings require every input tensor of an op to share the same batch dims (they do not broadcast), so these wrappers normalise inputs to a common broadcast batch shape and allocate outputs with that shape. The broadcast is done zero-copy: each input is re-strided to the target batch shape with 0-strides on the broadcast axes (a view that shares memory with the original), which the stride-aware C++ library consumes directly without any copy. Returned outputs therefore carry the broadcast batch shape.

Read-only inputs are likewise passed with their native strides (no contiguous copy is forced); only freshly allocated outputs and in-place (_-suffixed) buffers are materialised as contiguous arrays.

Spline order and boundary condition arguments accept an int, one of the re-exported :class:Spline / :class:Bound enums, or a friendly string (e.g. "cubic", "dct2").

The implementation is split by category into :mod:._util (validation and batch-broadcast helpers), :mod:._dt (distance transforms), :mod:._sym (compact-symmetric linear algebra), :mod:._resample (spline coefficients and resampling), :mod:._pushpull (spline gather/scatter) and :mod:._reg (spatial regularisers).

What this wrapper deliberately does not expose

Of the 58 public operations of the C++ hub, this package wraps all but four. tools/api_inventory.py in fastfields-dlpack prints the full matrix; the omissions are:

pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward, grad_backward The adjoints of the pushpull operators, with respect to both the sampled field and the sampling coordinates. They exist so that an autograd engine can differentiate through grid, which only :mod:fastfields.torch has; there is no automatic differentiation on numpy, so a wrapper here would be a bare function nothing calls, with five pre-zeroed buffers for the caller to get right. They stay reachable through the raw bindings -- fastfields.dlpack.pull_backward(...) and friends -- which is the honest layer for them.

This is checked rather than asserted: tests/test_api_coverage.py fails if the set of operations this package omits ever differs from the list above.

Solve (M + R) x = grd by preconditioned conjugate gradients.

The Krylov alternative to :func:field_relax's Gauss-Seidel sweeps on the same system, Jacobi-preconditioned by :func:field_precond's (M + diag(R))^-1.

sol is both the warm start and the output: it is mutated in place and returned, exactly like :func:field_relax. Pass a zero-filled array for a cold start, or a previous estimate to continue from it.

Iteration stops after nb_iter steps, or as soon as the relative residual drops below tol (tol <= 0 runs every iteration), or early if the operator turns out not to be positive definite along the current search direction. Pass return_info=True to find out which happened.

Notes

This operation is CPU-only in fastfields-lib (its dot products need a device-side reduction the CUDA backend does not implement yet, fastfields-lib#34). That costs this wrapper nothing -- numpy arrays are host memory -- but it is why fastfields.cupy has no field_cg.

items.title: fastfields.torch
items.text:
fastfields.torch: an autograd-enabled torch interface over the bindings.

A user-friendly, autograd-enabled torch interface over the fastfields.dlpack bindings.

Public API

Differentiable (torch.autograd.Function-backed):

  • :func:sym_matvec -- mat @ vec (grad wrt mat and vec)
  • :func:sym_solve -- (mat + diag(weight)) \ vec (grad wrt vec)
  • :func:sym_solve_ -- in-place :func:sym_solve (grad wrt the mutated right-hand side; safe under autograd, see API_CONTRACT.md)
  • :func:resample -- spline prolongation (backward: restriction)
  • :func:restriction-- adjoint of resample (backward: resample)
  • :func:spline_coeff -- interpolating-coefficient prefilter

  • :func:spline_coeff_ -- in-place :func:spline_coeff (self-adjoint, safe under autograd)

  • :func:pull, :func:push -- spline gather/scatter (grad wrt the field and the sampling grid)

  • :func:count -- splat ones (grad wrt grid)
  • :func:grad -- sample spatial gradients (grad wrt the field and grid; this is the second-order term a learned deformation needs)
  • the regulariser operators: :func:field_matvec / :func:flow_matvec, their _add/_sub accumulate forms over the operator, the diagonal and the stencil, :func:field_forward / :func:field_precond and their flow twins

Not differentiable, but still exposed for parity with fastfields.numpy/fastfields.cupy: forward always runs (even when an input requires grad), and only calling .backward() through the output raises a clear RuntimeError naming the op -- see each function's docstring, and API_CONTRACT.md ("In-place policy") for why this differs from earlier revisions that omitted these ops or rejected grad-requiring inputs at call time:

  • :func:dt_euclidean, :func:dt_euclidean_
  • :func:dt_l1, :func:dt_l1_
  • :func:dt_mesh (no in-place form on any backend)
  • :func:dt_spline_table, :func:dt_spline_brent, :func:dt_spline_gaussnewton -- the value at an argmin found by an inner optimisation, which the library does not differentiate
  • :func:sym_invert, :func:sym_invert_
  • :func:sym_addmatvec_, :func:sym_submatvec_ -- differentiable wrt the accumulator, but not wrt mat/vec; the out-of-place out0 + sym_matvec(mat, vec) is differentiable wrt all three

Re-exported enums: :class:Spline, :class:Bound.

What this wrapper deliberately does not expose

Of the 58 public operations of the C++ hub, this package wraps all but nine. tools/api_inventory.py in fastfields-dlpack prints the full matrix; the omissions are:

pull_backward, push_backward, count_backward, grad_backward, sym_matvec_backward Used, not re-exported. These are the adjoints behind the autograd.Function of the corresponding forward op, which is the supported way to reach them: call :func:pull / :func:push / :func:count / :func:grad / :func:sym_matvec and .backward(). Re-exporting them as functions would mean a second, unchecked spelling of a gradient computation, with five pre-zeroed buffers and an accumulate-vs-overwrite contract for the caller to get right. fastfields.dlpack has them raw for anyone who wants that.

field_precond_, flow_precond_, field_cg In-place preconditioner solves and the CG driver. The in-place forms would have to resolve against autograd's rules for a mutated buffer (API_CONTRACT.md, "In-place policy") and field_cg runs an iterative solver whose gradient is a solve with the same operator -- both worth doing, neither a mechanical wrapper, and both separate from exposing the ops. :func:field_relax is the differentiable-free in-place solver available today; fastfields.numpy has all three.

The implementation is split by category into :mod:._util (shared helpers and CUDA-stream resolution), :mod:._dt (distance transforms), :mod:._sym (compact-symmetric linear algebra), :mod:._resample (spline coefficients and resampling/restriction), :mod:._pushpull (spline gather/scatter) and :mod:._reg (spatial regularisers).

Differentiable wrt inp and grid. grad is itself a derivative operator, so its adjoint contributes second-order terms -- which is the point: an image gradient computed inside a loss has to be differentiable for the deformation that produced grid to be learnable.

In-place interpolating spline-coefficient prefilter, last axis.

Differentiable with respect to inp_out (mirrors :func:spline_coeff): the prefilter is linear, so its backward applies the prefilter's transpose to the gradient and never reads the pre-mutation inp_out -- only the saved order/bound scalars -- so overwriting inp_out in place destroys no information backward needs (see API_CONTRACT.md, "In-place policy"). sym_solve_(inp_out: Tensor, mat: Tensor, weight: Optional[Tensor] = None) -> Tensor

In-place solve: inp_out <- (mat + diag(weight)) \ inp_out.

Note the argument order -- inp_out first, then mat -- matches the numpy/cupy sym_solve_ convention, not :func:sym_solve's (mat, vec, ...) order.

Differentiable with respect to inp_out (mirrors :func:sym_solve); weight is a constant and mat must not require grad (as in :func:sym_solve). Safe under autograd: the backward of :func:sym_solve never reads the pre-mutation right-hand side -- only the saved mat/weight -- so overwriting inp_out in place destroys no information backward needs (see API_CONTRACT.md, "In-place policy"). As with any in-place op, a leaf tensor with requires_grad=True cannot be mutated (torch's ordinary leaf rule).
